description: The Buddha's life, the Four Sights, dependent origination and the Three Marks of Existence.
content_html:
The Life of the Buddha

Buddhism began with the life of the Buddha, Siddhattha Gotama, believed to have lived in what is now Nepal and northern India. The Buddhavamsa XXVI tells how Siddhattha was born into a noble family. A prophecy said he would either become a great king or a great spiritual teacher. His father, hoping to keep him on the kingly path, sheltered him from all suffering — surrounding him with luxury, beauty and youth.

Despite his father’s efforts, Siddhattha ventured outside the palace walls and encountered the Four Sights: an old man, a sick man, a corpse, and a wandering ascetic (a holy man living without possessions). The first three showed him the reality of suffering; the fourth showed him that a different path was possible. These encounters changed everything. Siddhattha left his palace, his wife and his infant son to pursue spiritual liberation.

Key Fact

According to the Buddhavamsa XXVI, the Four Sights were: an old man (ageing), a sick man (illness), a corpse (death) and a wandering ascetic (the possibility of transcending suffering). They prompted Siddhattha’s ‘great renunciation’ — leaving his privileged life to seek enlightenment.

Enlightenment and the Founding of the Sangha

After years of studying with teachers and practising extreme asceticism, Siddhattha concluded that neither luxury nor extreme self-denial led to liberation. He chose a Middle Way between the two. Sitting in meditation beneath a Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya, he attained enlightenment. He became the Buddha — the Awakened One.

After his enlightenment the Buddha travelled to the Deer Park at Isipatana (near modern Varanasi) and gave his first teaching to five former companions. This event is called the ‘Setting in Motion of the Wheel of the Dhamma’. From this gathering, the Sangha (the community) began to form. Together with the Buddha and the Dhamma (the teachings), the Sangha forms the Three Refuges — the foundation of Buddhist life.

Dependent Origination (Paticca-samuppada)

At the heart of the Buddha’s insight was paticca-samuppada, often translated as ‘dependent origination’ or conditionality. This teaching says that nothing exists on its own — everything arises because of other conditions, and when those conditions change, the thing itself changes or ceases. Ignorance leads to mental formations, which lead to consciousness, which leads to birth, ageing, sickness and death — a chain of twelve interconnected links that keeps beings caught in suffering.

Understanding dependent origination is liberating: if suffering arises from conditions, then changing those conditions can end suffering. This is the practical logic behind all Buddhist practice.

The Three Marks of Existence

The Buddha taught that all conditioned existence has three characteristics, known as the Three Marks of Existence:

Dukkha (suffering or unsatisfactoriness). Dukkha covers obvious physical pain, but also the subtler dissatisfaction of getting what we want but finding it does not truly satisfy, and the suffering caused by change — even pleasant things end.

Anicca (impermanence). Anicca means that nothing conditioned is permanent. Feelings, thoughts, relationships, physical health, the seasons — everything arises, changes and passes away. Clinging to things as if they were permanent is a fundamental cause of suffering.

Anatta (no fixed self). Anatta is perhaps the most challenging Mark. The Buddha taught that what we call ‘the self’ is not a fixed, permanent entity but a constantly changing collection of five aggregates (the khandas). There is no unchanging soul or essence at the core of a person.

The Milinda Panha (Questions of King Milinda) is an Edexcel-named anchor text. In it, the monk Nagasena explains anatta using the analogy of a chariot. He asks King Milinda: is the chariot the wheels? The axle? The frame? The pole? When you take away each component, no ‘chariot’ remains — the chariot only exists as a label given to the collection of parts. In the same way, what we call ‘a person’ is a collection of changing physical and mental processes. There is no fixed ‘self’ hidden inside. This is the teaching of anatta.

The story is not a denial that persons exist at all — Nagasena is clearly speaking to a real king. Rather, it shows that persons exist conventionally (as useful labels for collections of processes) but not ultimately (as fixed, eternal entities). This distinction is important for understanding Buddhist ethics and rebirth.

Key Fact

The Three Marks of Existence apply to all conditioned phenomena: dukkha (suffering/unsatisfactoriness), anicca (impermanence) and anatta (no fixed self). Understanding them deeply is essential for Buddhist practice because it removes the delusion that drives suffering.

Theravada Buddhism emphasises anatta strictly: there is no self at any level, and liberation involves the complete cessation of personal existence in nibbana. Mahayana Buddhism introduces the concept of sunyata (emptiness) — not just persons but all phenomena are empty of inherent existence. Some Mahayana traditions also speak of Buddha-nature (tathagatagarbha) as an innate capacity for awakening. These are not contradictions but different emphases on the same core insight.

This divergence matters for your 12-mark Discuss answers: a question about anatta or the self in Buddhism may expect you to contrast Theravada and Mahayana approaches.
exam_tip_html: For the ‘Outline three’ question, give three separate, distinct points — do not write three sentences developing one idea. For a question about the Three Marks, each mark is one brief point: dukkha, anicca, anatta. For the 5-mark ‘Explain two with sources’ question on this topic, the Milinda Panha (Story of Nagasena) is your named source — name it explicitly to earn the 5th mark. Do not just write ‘a Buddhist text says’. For the 12-mark Discuss, the most common error is treating anatta as simple nihilism (‘Buddhists think nothing exists’) — it is more subtle: persons exist conventionally but have no fixed, unchanging essence. SPaG marks reward correct spelling of ‘anicca’, ‘anatta’ and ‘paticca-samuppada’.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Buddha was Siddhattha Gotama; the Four Sights prompted his renunciation and the Buddhavamsa XXVI records the account. After enlightenment he taught the Dhamma and founded the Sangha.
  • Paticca-samuppada (dependent origination) teaches that all phenomena arise from conditions — nothing exists independently, and changing conditions can end suffering.
  • The Three Marks of Existence are dukkha (suffering), anicca (impermanence) and anatta (no fixed self). The Milinda Panha’s chariot analogy is the key named source for anatta.

practice_questions.text: Outline three events from the life of the Buddha that are important to Buddhists today.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for three separate, identified events. Acceptable points include: birth into a noble family foretold to lead to spiritual greatness; the Four Sights (encountering old age, sickness, death and a wandering ascetic); leaving the palace (the Great Renunciation); practising extreme asceticism then choosing the Middle Way; attaining enlightenment under the Bodhi tree; giving the first teaching at the Deer Park; founding the Sangha.

practice_questions.text: Describe the teaching of paticca-samuppada (dependent origination).
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks for accurate description. Acceptable content: paticca-samuppada means that all phenomena arise in dependence on conditions (1 mark); nothing exists independently or permanently (1 mark); when conditions change, phenomena change or cease (1 mark); it explains how ignorance leads through a chain of conditions to suffering, and how changing those conditions can end suffering (1 mark for development beyond basic definition — max 3 marks total).

practice_questions.text: Explain two of the Three Marks of Existence and why they are important for Buddhists.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per mark (1 for identification + development, 2 for full development). Example responses: Anicca (impermanence) — all conditioned things constantly change and eventually pass away; clinging to them as permanent causes suffering, so recognising anicca helps Buddhists reduce attachment. Anatta (no fixed self) — there is no permanent, unchanging self or soul; the ‘self’ is a label for a changing collection of processes; understanding anatta undermines ego-driven craving that causes suffering.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which the Milinda Panha helps Buddhists understand the teaching of anatta.
In your answer, include a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 + 2 marks for two developed explanations, +1 for a named source. The Milinda Panha is the named source for the 5th mark. Point 1: the chariot analogy shows that a person, like a chariot, is a label for a collection of parts — take away each part and no permanent ‘self’ remains. Point 2: the dialogue between Nagasena and King Milinda illustrates that persons exist conventionally but not ultimately — this helps Buddhists understand anatta without nihilism. 5th mark: ‘In the Milinda Panha, Nagasena uses the chariot analogy to explain to King Milinda that no fixed self exists’.

practice_questions.text:
'The Three Marks of Existence are the most important Buddhist teachings.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; weighs perspectives explicitly; conclusion justifies a clear position. Arguments in support: the Three Marks are the foundation of the Buddha's diagnosis of the human condition — understanding dukkha, anicca and anatta is the starting point for all Buddhist practice; the Milinda Panha anchors the teaching of anatta with a named authoritative source; dependent origination and the Three Marks together explain why life involves suffering and what can be done. Arguments against: the Four Noble Truths are sometimes seen as more practically central as they diagnose suffering AND prescribe the solution (the Eightfold Path); the Three Refuges (Buddha, Dhamma, Sangha) give structure to daily Buddhist life and may matter more practically; Mahayana Buddhists might prioritise the Bodhisattva ideal or sunyata over the Three Marks. Secure (7-9): Both sides present with some development; at least the Milinda Panha named. Developing (4-6): One side only or very brief treatment of the other. Emerging (1-3): One-sided or very brief.

practice_questions.text: Outline three ways in which the Buddha's enlightenment is significant for Buddhists today.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for three separate points. Acceptable: the enlightenment proved it is possible for a human being to achieve liberation from suffering; it established the Dhamma as an authoritative body of teaching; it led to the founding of the Sangha community; it provides a model for Buddhist practice — following the Buddha’s Middle Way; it is commemorated at the festival of Wesak; it shows that nibbana can be reached in this lifetime.

knowledge_checks.q: Which text specifically records the account of the Buddha's ancestry, birth and the Four Sights?
Which of the following CORRECTLY describes the teaching of anatta?
options: There is no such thing as a person at all
The self is a permanent, eternal soul hidden inside the body
What we call a person is a changing collection of physical and mental elements, not a fixed self
Only monks can understand the true self through meditation

knowledge_checks.q: In the Milinda Panha, the monk Nagasena uses the analogy of a _____ to explain the teaching of anatta to King Milinda.
The Three Marks of Existence are dukkha, anatta and _____.
Match each term to its correct meaning:
right: The teaching that all phenomena arise in dependence on conditions
The unsatisfactory, suffering nature of conditioned existence

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'Buddhavamsa XXVI' record about the Buddha's life?
flashcard_questions.a: The ancestry, birth, princely life, Four Sights and enlightenment of Siddhattha Gotama.

flashcard_questions.q: What were the Four Sights that prompted the Buddha to renounce his palace life?
flashcard_questions.a: An old man, a sick man, a corpse and a wandering ascetic.
A Pali text recording Nagasena's dialogue with King Milinda; it explains anatta using the chariot analogy.

flashcard_questions.q: What analogy does Nagasena use to explain anatta in the Milinda Panha?
flashcard_questions.a: A chariot: take away each part and no 'chariot' remains — persons likewise have no fixed self.
Dependent origination: all phenomena arise in dependence on conditions and cease when conditions change.
The First Mark of Existence: the suffering and unsatisfactoriness of conditioned existence.
The Second Mark of Existence: impermanence — all conditioned phenomena constantly change.
The Third Mark of Existence: no fixed self — the 'self' is a changing collection, not a permanent entity.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the Three Refuges in Buddhism?
flashcard_questions.a: The Buddha, the Dhamma (teachings) and the Sangha (community).

flashcard_questions.q: Where did the Buddha give his first teaching after enlightenment?
flashcard_questions.a: The Deer Park at Isipatana (near Varanasi), to five former companions.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the key difference between Theravada and Mahayana views on the self?
flashcard_questions.a: Theravada: strict anatta. Mahayana: also sunyata (emptiness) and, in some schools, Buddha-nature.
The community of Buddhist monks, nuns and lay practitioners; one of the Three Refuges.

glossary_terms.definition: The title meaning 'the Awakened One', given to Siddhattha Gotama after his enlightenment; the founder of Buddhism.
An ancient Pali text that recounts the histories of previous Buddhas and the life of Gotama, including the Four Sights.
The four experiences that prompted Siddhattha Gotama to leave his palace life: an old man, a sick man, a corpse and a wandering ascetic.
Spiritual awakening; the state of having understood the true nature of reality and been freed from greed, hatred and delusion.
The community of Buddhist monks, nuns and lay practitioners; one of the Three Refuges.
The teachings of the Buddha; also the nature of reality or the truth of how things are.
Dependent origination: the Buddhist teaching that all phenomena arise in dependence on conditions and nothing exists independently.
An ancient Pali text recording a dialogue between the monk Nagasena and King Milinda, used to illustrate the teaching of anatta.
The First Mark of Existence: the unsatisfactory, suffering nature of conditioned existence.
The Second Mark of Existence: the teaching that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent and constantly changing.
The Third Mark of Existence: the teaching that there is no permanent, unchanging self; what we call a person is a changing collection of elements.
The older of the two main Buddhist traditions, predominant in Sri Lanka, Thailand and Southeast Asia; emphasises the individual path to nibbana.
The broader Buddhist tradition that emphasises the Bodhisattva ideal of helping all beings to liberation; includes Pure Land, Zen and Tibetan forms.
